data.title: OpenAI's chief scientist proposes industry limits on AI development
data.description:
By Jorgelina do Rosario
 
OpenAI’s chief scientist proposed that artificial intelligence companies agree to limits on developing increasingly powerful models until researchers have better ways to understand and monitor their behavior.
 
Jakub Pachocki called for industrywide standards that would establish thresholds for AI development, with companies agreeing not to exceed them until specific safety requirements are met, according to a post published Sunday.
 
“I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone,” Pachocki wrote.
 
The proposed limits could be based partly on a technical measurement known as perplexity, which gauges how well an AI model predicts the next piece of text. Pachocki didn’t specify what the initial limit should be or when it might take effect.
 
 
Pachocki warned that AI could accelerate advances in its own development as soon as 2027, potentially outpacing improvements in researchers’ ability to monitor and understand the technology.
 
OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman endorsed the proposal, calling Pachocki’s essay “the most important thing OpenAI has published in awhile.” He said in a post on X that agreeing to common limits would help ensure “safety and control.”
 
The proposal comes as the US prepares for renewed debate over AI regulation following Democrats’ sweeping victories in the midterm elections. The party’s gains in the House, Senate and governors’ races could bring greater congressional scrutiny of technology companies and renewed efforts to establish AI safety rules.
 
Some lawmakers are also discussing the creation of a dedicated Senate committee to coordinate AI policy. President Donald Trump has opposed broad restrictions on AI development, setting up a potential clash with the incoming Democratic Congress over how to regulate the technology.

data.title: India's armed forces turn to startups to build battlefield tech at speed
data.description:
India’s armed forces are turning to domestic startups for technology that can be developed and deployed quickly during conflicts, ranging from firefighting robots and underwater vision cameras to autonomous underwater vehicles.
 
At the Bengaluru Tech Summit, officials from the Army, Navy, Air Force, and iDEX (Innovations for Defence Excellence), the Department of Defence Production’s innovation initiative, said closer industry collaboration, co-development, and funding support could help address gaps in manufacturing, artificial intelligence (AI), and technology sovereignty.
 
A key challenge for startups is moving from working prototypes to large-scale production. Officials also stressed that human oversight must remain central to defence AI.
 
India spent $92.1 billion on its military in 2025, up 8.9 per cent from 2024, making it the world’s fifth-largest military spender, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
 
The institute credited the rise partly to the May 2025 conflict with Pakistan, which involved combat aircraft, drones, and missiles.
 
“Our role has changed from interacting with or purchasing equipment to co-developing with startups and industries,” said Wing Commander Gaddam Sandeep, commanding officer of the Regional Aerospace Innovation Division in Bengaluru.
 
Beyond the prototype
 
Vipin Yadav, deputy programme director at iDEX, said India’s defence startup ecosystem faces a gap between technology readiness and the ability to manufacture products at scale. “When we are ready for a product, it doesn’t mean we will be able to deliver it in huge numbers,” he said.
 
iDEX provides grants to early-stage startups and offers minimum pilot order quantities to give them visibility on potential orders after product validation. It has also introduced measures to help startups build business cases and secure repeat orders.
 
Grants alone may not be enough to establish production lines, said Commodore S K Singh, officer in charge of the Indian Navy’s Technology Development Acceleration Cell, which identifies capability gaps and works with startups to address them.
 
Under the Defence Acquisition Procedure, startups working with iDEX and the Technology Development Fund, with cumulative contract values of up to ₹250 crore, can access incentives including using intellectual property as collateral, advances of up to 15 per cent of the base contract value, and payments covering 100 per cent of raw material costs against invoices or committed purchases. They may also receive exemptions from liquidated damages.
 
The armed forces do not prevent startups from selling dual-use products commercially, Singh said. He cited a firefighting robot developed with a ₹1.5 crore grant that has since secured orders from the Army, Navy, Air Force, and oil and gas companies.
 
Co-development can also expand a product’s capabilities. The Navy initially approached a startup to build an AI-powered underwater vision camera for visibility in turbid waters. The project later expanded to include an echo sounder, sonar, and metal detector. The Navy inducted the integrated system, which Singh described as world-class. The startup subsequently adapted the technology for an autonomous underwater vehicle, enabling persistent underwater operations.
 
The Navy is working with around 150 startups, more than 30 of them in Bengaluru, Singh said. Sandeep said Karnataka accounts for more than 65 per cent of India's aerospace and AI industries. He called for centralised testing facilities and a hub-and-spoke model connecting startups with established aerospace companies.
 
AI built for the front lines
 
“The focus should not be on building larger AI models. It should be more on application-based small models which can help services in decision-making and surveillance,” Yadav said.
 
Sandeep said defence AI must evolve beyond prototypes because battlefield conditions and enemy tactics keep changing. Models need rapid iterations and testing in extreme temperatures and actual operational environments. “We don’t want huge computational models. We want small models, but it needs to have iterations faster,” he said.
 
The Navy needs task-specific models that can operate with limited data, power, and computing capacity, Singh said. Ships have restricted bandwidth when communicating with shore stations and can remain on patrol for two to three months, making frequent software updates difficult. The Navy therefore wants systems that can process data at the edge and detect rare events after long periods of inactivity.
 
Sandeep urged startups entering aviation to begin by modernising the Air Force’s legacy systems, some of which are 30 to 40 years old. They must also be prepared to maintain and support products throughout their 30-40-year service life.
 
Who owns the battlefield brain?
 
Access to classified data remains another challenge. Singh said the Navy wants developers to work alongside its personnel at naval facilities. Sandeep said the Air Force could share open-source and legacy data during development, but classified data would remain with the service once a model enters the defence domain. Further development would take place in a sandbox environment.
 
Lieutenant Colonel Sumanto Lahiri, officer in charge of the Indian Army Cell at the Army Design Bureau, said indigenous computing capabilities were essential to technology sovereignty. “Nobody is stopping us from developing our own sovereign software stacks,” he said.
 
The Navy has also launched a sovereign AI challenge through iDEX, requiring participating companies to transfer intellectual property rights and software to the service. The challenge attracted 68 industry proposals, Singh said.
 
Humans hold the trigger
 
Officials said AI would not replace human accountability in military operations. Lahiri said the Army had no scope for fully autonomous, AI-driven decision-making. “It is always human in the loop. The final call is taken by the human,” he said.
 
Singh said AI could independently support observation and surveillance, but human oversight would remain necessary for decisions and actions until the Navy developed sufficient confidence in the technology.
 
“AI is just an enabler. It’s not a decision maker,” Sandeep said. 
Building India’s next-gen arsenal
 
  • Firefighting robots, underwater vision systems, autonomous vehicles move into military’s tech pipeline
  • Scaling prototypes into mass production remains a key battle for defence startups
  • Military seeks lean, task-specific AI models for battlefield conditions
  • Indigenous computing, sovereign software emerge as critical lines of defence
  • AI may scan the battlefield, but humans control military decisions

data.title: RBI Act may show the way on Tata Sons listing amid regulatory uncertainty
data.description:
Will the shareholders of Tata Sons, the holding company of the salt-to-software conglomerate, have the final say on the company’s proposed stock exchange listing, or will the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) mandate on compulsory listing prevail? Domain experts are scanning the RBI Act, which was enacted in 1934 and amended several times thereafter, to find an answer to that question, which is at the centre of the biggest corporate battle of the time.
 
Even as an amendment of the Articles of Association (AoA) of Tata Sons in the case of listing would require a special resolution passed by at least 75 per cent shareholders, sources believe listing is “imminent”. One of the sources, without wanting to be quoted, pointed at the sequence of events and also the various clauses of the RBI Act to state that non-compliance with directions of the central bank could have civil and criminal implications for the business of the company and its management. He added that the impact could be felt by the entire Tata group, and not just Tata Sons.
 
The forthcoming board meeting of Tata Sons on November 26 is expected to take up the company’s listing proposal. Some board members may assert that non-compliance with the RBI direction is not possible. Tata Trusts Chairman and Nominee Director Noel Tata has, however, already said that the alternative plan to restructure Tata Sons — so that it can remain private — would have to be discussed at the meeting.
 
The RBI identified Tata Sons as an upper layer non-banking financial company (NBFC) in 2022, after which, the company paid off all its debts and applied for deregistration as a core investment company in 2024. On September 11, 2026, the banking regulator rejected the Tata Sons application, while asking it to comply immediately. On November 16, 2026, it reiterated that the company must list, as is required of an upper layer NBFC. 
 
The RBI Act, ranging from Section 45 to Section 58, mentions the consequences of non-compliance, according to a domain expert. For instance, the regulator may cancel the certificate of registration (CoR), after providing a reasonable opportunity of hearing. Carrying on with business as an NBFC without the certificate of registration is an offence with imprisonment and financial penalty provisions.
 
There could be curbs on dealing with assets due to non-compliance with RBI directive. For an investment holding company, this could freeze divestments, block sales, stake dilutions and pledges across the group.
 
There’s a provision for removal of directors also to ensure financial stability or securing proper management in the public interest. According to a source, in Tata Son’s case, “public interest” and “proper management” are important clauses, and could affect any director where the relevant clause is applicable. Supersession of the board of directors for up to five years can be enforced as well for these reasons.
 
Under the RBI Act, imprisonment for a term of up to three years can also be given to persons in charge of and responsible for the conduct of business.
 
Sonam Chandwani, managing partner at KS Legal & Associates, told Business Standard that shareholders may decide whether they want the company to remain private, but the decision on its regulatory status rests with the RBI. “Shareholders cannot override or dilute the RBI’s independent regulatory mandate,” she said. As for the alternative plan mooted by Noel Tata, the RBI would have to examine the business post-restructuring before reconsidering its classification, Chandwani explained.  
 
“I do not think the RBI will resort to any harsh or punitive action against Tata Sons at this stage. The regulator’s approach is likely to be continued engagement, with discussions between the RBI and the management ongoing, persuading the latter to make a decision on compliance,’’ said Abizer Diwanji, founder, NeoStrat Advisors. Tata Sons may also point out that listing cannot happen overnight and would require time, including discussions with shareholders on a proposed plan, he said. “If the matter reaches serious confrontation, the ultimate recourse could ultimately be judicial, leaving the question of the RBI’s interpretation and jurisdiction to the courts.” But the management is expected to remain responsive to RBI’s concerns, he said.  
 
The RBI did not respond to a query from Business Standard on the matter.

data.title: To list or not to list: Noel Tata wants Tata Sons Nov 26 board meet deferred
data.description:
Tata Trusts chairman and nominee director on the Tata Sons board, Noel Tata, is learnt to have asked the group's holding company to defer the board meeting scheduled for November 26. The board agenda was uploaded over the weekend, with less than a week to go before the meeting. Tata Sons is expected to defer the board meeting, and a fresh date will be decided soon.
 
The next board meeting, the first after the September 17 face-off between the Tata Sons directors and Noel Tata, is likely to be stormy as well. The proposed listing of Tata Sons would come up at the next board meeting amid opposition from Noel, it is learnt. The discussion assumes greater significance against the backdrop of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) reiterating that listing is mandatory for Tata Sons as an upper-layer non-banking financial company (NBFC).
 
 
Noel Tata, in a recent letter, has maintained that the alternative plan to keep Tata Sons private must be discussed at the upcoming board meeting. The plan, mooted by Noel, involves merging two group operating companies — Tata Electronics Systems Solutions (TESS) and Tata Consulting Engineers (TCE) — into Tata Sons so that the company does not qualify as a core investment company or an upper-layer NBFC.
 
While any listing proposal has to go to shareholders for their approval, experts believe that shareholders cannot override or dilute regulatory compliance. Clarity on this front is likely to emerge in a few days after the next board meeting. The RBI had classified Tata Sons as an upper-layer NBFC in 2022, giving it three years to comply — that is, mandatorily go for a stock market listing. However, Tata Sons cleared its debt and applied to deregister from the core investment company (CIC) category in 2024. In September 2026, the RBI rejected Tata Sons' application, asking it to comply with its directive immediately. Then, in November 2026, it again reiterated that Tata Sons must list.
 
On September 17, the Tata Sons board meeting had turned into a boardroom battle, with all directors other than Noel backing a third term for N Chandrasekaran as executive chairman of the company. In the voting that followed, two nominee directors — Noel Tata and Venu Srinivasan — went against each other, resulting in a casting vote by independent director Harish Manwani, who was chairing the discussion. The listing of Tata Sons was not put to a vote, but the entire board, other than Noel, backed the proposal.

data.title: Cyber insurance market likely to treble in 5 years: Deloitte report
data.description:
India’s cyber insurance market is expected to nearly treble over the next five years as digitalisation, rising cyber threats and interconnected financial services increase businesses’ exposure to cyber risks, according to a Deloitte report.
 
The market is projected to reach $321-594 million by 2030-31 (FY31), growing at an annual rate of 18-19 per cent from $115-255 million in FY25. Growth is expected to be driven by rising cyber incidents, cloud adoption, digital payments and data protection requirements, as well as demand from financial institutions, technology companies, healthcare providers, digital platforms and micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs).
 
Aggregate insured limits in India have grown by an estimated 16-17 per cent annually over the past three years. Some large banking policyholders nearly doubled their limits between FY25 and FY26, with coverage reaching $50-100 million in certain cases.
 
“Compared with five to seven years earlier, limits for some large banking policyholders may be as much as ten times higher,” the report said.
 
Large technology and IT-enabled services companies have purchased coverage of around $200-300 million, reflecting their exposure to operational disruption, data loss and third-party liabilities. Life sciences and pharmaceutical companies are also seeking higher protection against data breaches, privacy liabilities and business interruption.
 
The banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI) sector remains particularly vulnerable. Reserve Bank of India data indicates that digital payment fraud is rising, driven by social engineering and account takeovers. At least 116 data-related incidents were recorded across India's financial sector between March and August 2026, including 46 data breaches, 37 data leaks and 33 credit-card-related incidents.
 
The report flagged the growing vulnerability of cloud providers, shared technology providers and digital asset platforms in the financial sector, warning that cyber threats would become increasingly sophisticated.
 
The financial impact is also mounting. Industry estimates suggest cybercrime-related losses in India could exceed $20 billion annually as digital payments, cloud adoption and interconnected systems expand.
 
The insurance sector faces growing exposure from the rapid expansion of digital public infrastructure (DPI), including Aadhaar, UPI, Account Aggregator frameworks and API-enabled financial services. These systems allow insurers to scale policy issuance and servicing, but also increase the complexity of interconnected networks.
 
Despite rising exposure, cyber insurance penetration remains low, particularly among small and medium enterprises (SMEs), due to limited awareness, affordability concerns and evolving underwriting standards. This gap presents an opportunity for insurers to expand through risk-based underwriting and cyber-resilience solutions.
 
Further, on the insurance sector’s preparedness for the upcoming Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, Debashish Banerjee, partner and insurance sector leader at Deloitte South Asia, noted that while the framework does not mandate cyber insurance, companies can cover DPDP-related losses under existing policies. However, insurers must be able to assess whether a company’s cybersecurity resilience programme and DPDP compliance mechanisms are sufficiently robust.
 
“Companies will increasingly seek coverage for DPDP-related liabilities, and insurers will have to determine how to accommodate these requirements and price the associated risks. This makes it important for insurers to establish clear inclusion and exclusion criteria. They must identify which risks they are willing to underwrite and which industries or organisations offer a more acceptable risk profile. There is considerable market potential in cyber insurance and with accurate risk assessment and underwriting right policies can build a profitable portfolio,” he said
 
Insurers are increasingly factoring cybersecurity preparedness, identity protection, vulnerability management, incident response and third-party risks into underwriting. Continuous monitoring of vulnerabilities and changes in a policyholder’s risk exposure could eventually influence coverage, premiums and policy terms, although dynamic pricing remains an evolving approach.
 
“In cyber insurance insurers need more data to understand the probability of an attack, the potential financial impact and the likely payout. An insurance company must determine how much premium it should charge for a particular level of risk. The lack of adequate historical data makes this underwriting process difficult. The second challenge is the ability to conduct effective risk assessments of individual organizations. Similarly, cyber insurers need detailed information about a company's cybersecurity infrastructure,” said Munjal Kamdar, partner, Deloitte India.
 
“However, many organizations do not even maintain an inventory of all their digital assets or third-party vendors. Without this information, insurance companies cannot accurately assess the organization's cyber risk or determine appropriate premiums. Therefore, the industry needs better risk assessment models, more comprehensive data points and greater underwriting sophistication to unlock the market's growth potential,” he added.
 
The report also flagged a data gap: cyber insurance premiums and claims are not separately reported as a standalone category in domestic industry statistics, making it difficult to assess the segment’s growth and penetration. Regulatory developments, including data protection requirements and cybersecurity guidelines for insurers, are expected to strengthen governance, incident reporting and operational resilience, further supporting market growth. 
In numbers 
 
  • $321-594 mn: Estimated size of India’s cyber insurance market by FY31
  • 18-19%: Expected annual market growth over five years
  • 16-17%: Annual growth in aggregate insured limits over the past three years
  • $50-100 mn: Cover for some large banking policyholders in FY26
  • $200-300 mn: Cyber cover bought by large technology and IT services firms
  • 116: Data-related incidents across the financial sector between March and August
  • $20 bn: Estimated annual cybercrime losses in India

data.title: Centre considers fertiliser subsidy sharing model amid rising costs
data.description:
Amid an exponential rise in fertiliser subsidy due to perceived diversion for non-farm use, the government has proposed to share the subsidy cost with states using a pre-fixed formula to ensure more oversight and judicious use.
 
Discussions over the proposal are at a nascent stage, as it could entail turning the urea subsidy into a Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) from the current Central Sector Scheme.
 
This would require significant legislative and budgetary changes, a new fund flow mechanism and Centre-state coordination.
 
But, on the positive-side it (subsidy-sharing) could ensure more vigil and also help in ensuring judicious use of fertilisers, an official explained.
 
A Central Sector programme is entirely funded by the Centre, and states do not share any financial responsibility towards it.
 
Urea is the largest component of India’s annual subsidy burden, having cornered around 68 per cent of India’s annual FY27 Budget Estimates (BE) for fertiliser subsidy projected at ₹1.70 trillion
 
It ensures that farmers receive fertilisers at a fixed maximum retail price (MRP), while manufacturers are compensated for the difference between the production cost or cost of import and the MRP.
 
If finally approved, the fertiliser subsidy expenditure may be shared between the Centre and the states in 70:30, or 60:40, or even 50:50 ratios, or whatever is mutually agreed upon by the two sides.
 
“See, there is an urgent need to reduce the Centre’s fertiliser subsidy burden and raising the retail price of items like urea is not a way out (as it would burden the farmers); therefore, one option could be to make states partners in sharing the burden because after all agriculture is a state subject,” the official said.
 
He said the concept (of expenditure sharing) has already been adopted now for Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin), or VB G RAM G, wherein the Centre and states share the wages expenditure in a 60:40 ratio, as against the earlier format under MGNREGA wherein the Centre bore 100 per cent of the unskilled wage expenditure.
 
“The same could also be thought of for the fertiliser subsidy, provided the states agree and are on board,” the official explained.
 
MGNREGA, which was reformed into VB G RAM G, has been implemented across India since July 1, 2026.
 
The drag on fertiliser subsidy is significant: Data shows that as of November 16, with about four and a half months remaining in FY27, the Centre has already exhausted 86 per cent of its Budgeted fertiliser subsidy allocation of around ₹1.71 trillion.
 
It also shows that till November 16, 2026, the Centre has spent around ₹1.46 trillion on fertiliser subsidy; with a significant chunk going towards payment for urea imports.
 
As against the re-appropriated Budget allocation of around ₹44,001 crore for subsiding imported urea, a sum of around  ₹43,245.55 crore (around 98.28 per cent) has already been spent until November 16.
 
When it comes to subsidy on indigenous production of urea, sources said against a reassessed sum of ₹86,635 crore allocated in the Budget for FY27, an expenditure of around ₹61,825.22 crore (around 71.36 per cent) had already been made until November 16.
 
As regards subsidy on P&K fertilisers both for indigenous production and also imports, sources said against a re-appropriated Budget allocation of ₹54,000 crore, a sum of around ₹21,256.45 crore (or around 76.24 per cent) had been exhausted till November 16.
 
Urea is sold at a fixed rate of ₹267 per 45 kg bag to farmers while diammonium phosphate (DAP) is sold at a controlled rate of ₹1,350 per 50 kg bag.
 
Recently, the Centre had announced a sharp increase in per kg subsidy under the nutrient-based subsidy regime compared to both kharif this year and rabi last year totalling around ₹62,370.02 crore (more than 64 per cent jump from the previous rabi season) with sulphur getting the maximum hike of over 220 per cent.

data.title: Delhi air quality remains poor as AQI rises, forecast signals no respite
data.description:
Delhi’s air quality remained in the ‘poor’ category on Monday, with the city recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 248 at 7 am, according to real-time data from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB). PM2.5 continued to be the prominent pollutant.
 
The city-level reading was 12 points higher than the AQI of 236 reported at 9 am on Sunday. Pollution levels varied considerably across the capital. Of the 58 monitoring stations with valid readings at 7 am, 51 recorded AQI levels above 200, while five reported readings above 300, placing them in the ‘very poor’ category.
 
Sirifort recorded the highest AQI at 331, followed by NSUT Jaffarpur at 323 and IGNOU, Maidan Garhi, at 320. Talkatora Garden reported 315, while Pusa, monitored by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), recorded 312.
 
 
Among other locations, ITO recorded an AQI of 297, CRRI Mathura Road 296, Aya Nagar 295 and Burari Crossing 293. Commonwealth Sports Complex reported 291, while DTU recorded 288.
 
At the other end, Ghoga recorded the lowest AQI at 130, followed by Lodhi Road at 149 and IMD Lodhi Road at 161. These locations were in the ‘moderate’ category.

NCR cities report mixed air quality

Air quality across the National Capital Region (NCR) remained uneven. Rohtak in Haryana recorded an AQI of 248, the same as Delhi, while Ghaziabad reported 233 and Bhiwadi in Rajasthan 229.
 
Greater Noida recorded an AQI of 228, followed by Manesar at 217, Hapur at 216, Gurugram at 215 and Noida at 212. Bahadurgarh reported 197, while Meerut recorded 187.
 
Among other NCR cities, Bulandshahr reported an AQI of 178, Sonipat 174 and Baghpat 168. Faridabad recorded 136, while Bharatpur and Alwar reported 127 and 124, respectively. Panipat and Palwal were among the better-performing locations, with readings of 95 and 94.

Hanumangarh, Malegaon record highest AQI nationally

Among the 281 cities with valid readings in the CPCB’s 7 am dataset, Hanumangarh in Rajasthan and Malegaon in Maharashtra recorded the highest AQI at 276 each. Panchgaon in Haryana followed at 265, while Dharuhera recorded 264 and Bhiwani 261.
 
Udaipur in Rajasthan reported an AQI of 260, followed by Bikaner at 256. Rohtak and Delhi both recorded 248, while Khairthal in Rajasthan also reported 248. Gajraula in Uttar Pradesh recorded 241.
 
At the other end, Aizawl in Mizoram recorded the lowest AQI at 9, followed by Sasaram in Bihar at 17 and Gangtok in Sikkim at 27. Begusarai in Bihar reported 30, while Rairangpur in Odisha recorded 34. Ramgarh in Bihar, Gaya in Bihar and Bhilai in Chhattisgarh reported readings of 35 each.
 
Under the CPCB’s National Air Quality Index classification, readings between 0 and 50 are categorised as ‘good’, 51 and 100 as ‘satisfactory’, 101 and 200 as ‘moderate’, 201 and 300 as ‘poor’, 301 and 400 as ‘very poor’, and 401 and 500 as ‘severe’.

Forecast points to continued poor air quality

The latest available forecast from the Air Quality Warning and Integrated Decision Support System for Emissions - Delhi (AIRWISE-Delhi) indicates that the capital’s air quality is likely to remain in the ‘poor’ category from Monday to Wednesday, with the possibility of readings moving between ‘poor’ and ‘very poor’ over the following six days. Favourable winds and an increase in mixing depth had helped disperse pollutants over the weekend, but the improvement may not be sustained, according to a report by India Today citing the forecast.
 
The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) currently lists Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan (Grap) as active across Delhi-NCR. Under Stage II of Grap, measures including mechanised road sweeping, dust suppression, water sprinkling are taken along with stricter enforcement of dust-control norms at construction sites and restrictions on the use of personal vehicles.

data.title: Trump's description of Putin as a friend is entirely appropriate: DNI chief
data.description:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said Sunday it was "entirely appropriate" for President Donald Trump to call Russian leader Vladimir Putin his friend.

Clayton defended comments that Democrats have characterized as a betrayal of American values after Trump met with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping for rare three-way talks. The summit last week in China seemed to be more symbolism than substance, but Trump and his top aides have described it as a historic gathering of the three countries with the largest nuclear arsenals.

Trump raised eyebrows with his warm greeting of Putin and repeated references to him as his "friend," which continued on Saturday, when the Republican president posted an image on Truth Social of him shaking hands with a smiling Putin under the caption, "My Friend." "In that circle - in that circle of that conversation, using the term friend' is entirely appropriate," Clayton said on ABC's "This Week." He had a similar assessment on CNN's "State of the Union," where he said it was "historic" and "remarkable" for Trump to meet with the presidents of the other leading nuclear powers.

 

"In that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely," Clayton said.

Like Trump, Clayton declined when pressed to characterize Putin as a friend of the United States, noting Russia's invasion of Ukraine, an American ally.

"He is not America's friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all," Clayton said on ABC.

Trump's fondness for Putin has been a defining characteristic of Trump's two terms as president. He beamed when meeting the Russian leader last week. After returning to Washington, Trump made no effort in the White House briefing room on Friday to walk back the comments, and he noticeably sidestepped a specific question about whether he views Putin as a friend to the US.

"I can't speak to America," Trump said, then immediately shifted to his "very good" personal relationship with Putin.

"I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship (with)," Trump said. "It's actually very good." Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York criticized the summit as a "historic embarrassment" for the United States.

"America would have been far better off if Trump just stayed home," Schumer said from the Senate floor.

data.title: US tracked Alice Huang's links with China spy agency during Nvidia affair
data.description:
By Jonathan Swan, Julian E Barnes and Maggie Haberman
 
The Chinese woman at the heart of the Nvidia scandal kept in contact with an official of China’s top spy agency for more than a year while she was carrying out a secret affair with Jensen Huang, according to multiple people with knowledge of U.S. intelligence reports that describe the encounters.
 
The woman, Alice Huang, was in touch with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, the people with knowledge of the intelligence said. That period overlaps with at least a portion of the time she was in a relationship with Mr. Huang, then the head of the world’s leading maker of advanced artificial intelligence chips.
 
 
U.S. intelligence agencies have also gathered evidence that Ms. Huang’s business partner, Kang Wei, who was often introduced as her husband, worked with the same Chinese spy agency, the people said.
 
The extent and specific timing of Ms. Huang’s contacts with the spy agency — and Mr. Kang’s work for the same intelligence service — have not been previously reported.
 
Ms. Huang’s contacts with the Chinese spy agency last year and up through recent months help to flesh out how U.S. officials came to believe that Mr. Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive earlier this month, was the target of an intelligence operation.
 
They correspond not just to the time when he was conducting the affair but also to at least part of the period when Ms. Huang’s company, Megaspeed, was acquiring large amounts of advanced Nvidia chips, some of which went to data centers in Southeast Asia serving Chinese technology companies like Alibaba and some of which are suspected of being smuggled to China.
 
Allies of the former Nvidia chief, including President Trump, have sought to minimize the scandal and questioned whether Ms. Huang was spying for Chinese intelligence. But the newly revealed information underscores the continuous contacts that she had with the Ministry of State Security, even as she was in a romantic relationship with Mr. Huang.
 
It also helps to flesh out why some American officials have been worried that Ms. Huang’s role is just one element of a much broader push by China in that technological battle. The Ministry of State Security has prioritized focusing on acquiring high-end chips and advancing China’s A.I. ambitions.
 
U.S. officials are investigating the role of Ms. Huang and Mr. Kang in a network of Southeast Asian companies, including Megaspeed, that have been linked to the possible smuggling of Nvidia chips to China, to evade U.S. export control laws. U.S. officials are still working to determine the full extent and duration of their work with Chinese intelligence.
 
The intelligence gathered by the U.S. contains evidence — including shipping records — demonstrating the role of Ms. Huang and Mr. Kang in that network of companies, people with knowledge of the intelligence reports said. The New York Times has previously reported that Ms. Huang and her family have a web of connections to Chinese defense contractors.
 
Mr. Huang initially described his relationship with Ms. Huang as normal interactions with a business customer. He acknowledged an affair only after The Times revealed last month that Ms. Huang had been identified by the United States as a Chinese intelligence asset and that the Nvidia chief had been picked up on electronic surveillance targeting her.
 
He stepped down this month after The Times subsequently reported that he had an affair with a subordinate at Nvidia. Administration officials never provided him with a so-called defensive briefing about Ms. Huang, a heads-up that the woman he was in a relationship with had been linked to Chinese intelligence.
 
A spokesman for Mr. Huang declined to comment. The White House, the State Department, the Chinese Embassy in Washington, Ms. Huang and Mr. Kang did not respond to requests for comment on Sunday.
 
Before the scandal broke into public view, advisers to Mr. Trump told him on at least two occasions that U.S. intelligence had uncovered Ms. Huang’s links to the Chinese spy agency and that she was in a close relationship with Mr. Huang while he was still running Nvidia, according to U.S. officials with direct knowledge of the briefings.
 
Both times, including when his national security adviser discussed it with him, the president downplayed the concerns and made clear he did not want to intervene in the matter. The officials said Mr. Trump regarded Mr. Huang as a valuable ally and Nvidia as essential to the health of the American economy and stock market. Mr. Trump has recently suggested that Nvidia should consider bringing Mr. Huang back as chief executive, a possibility the company’s board has rejected.
 
“We have to protect our brilliant people. Jensen is one of them,” the president said at a White House news conference on Friday. “I think the company if they were smart they’d take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work.”
 
Mr. Trump has claimed that no one in his government told him of any intelligence indicating that Ms. Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset.
 
“I don’t know that she is a spy,” he said. “Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy.”
 
In fact, his administration has been monitoring Ms. Huang’s contacts with the Chinese spy agency for more than a year, a period when the Ministry of State Security has been intensifying its new role in seeking to give China an advantage in artificial intelligence.
 
“This network of companies working to procure and smuggle Nvidia chips lines up precisely with the M.S.S.’s recently stated core mission of circumventing and undermining U.S. export controls on semiconductors and other key technologies,” said Matt Pottinger, who served as deputy national security adviser during Mr. Trump’s first term, and who is chief executive of the open-source research firm Garnaut Global.
 
The Ministry of State Security has for decades declared that its mission is to combat espionage and to eliminate political threats to Communist Party rule in China. The minister of state security, Chen Yixin, gave a similar five-point statement as recently as late last year. Then in April, he unveiled a new, sixth mission — overcoming the “blockades” choking China’s access to key technologies like artificial intelligence.
 
“Deepen the struggle against blockades, and comprehensively advance artificial intelligence innovation, industry development and applications,” Mr. Chen wrote in a party journal. “Focus on tackling the ‘choke holds’ of critical technologies.”
 
“To assume the M.S.S. wasn’t at the center of this operation would be to assume that they are incompetent,” Mr. Pottinger added. “That’s not an assumption I would make.”
 
American spy agencies are still working to understand the role played by Mr. Kang, the business partner of Ms. Huang, whom she would introduce to associates as her husband. Multiple people with knowledge of the intelligence said the United States had collected evidence that Mr. Kang worked with the Ministry of State Security.
 
Ms. Huang also appears to have met with officials of China’s Ministry of Public Security, the nation’s main law enforcement agency, according to multiple people with knowledge of the U.S. intelligence reports.
 
Ms. Huang, Mr. Kang, Ms. Huang’s sister and companies associated with them have emerged as a significant branch of the Chinese effort to build data centers and acquire access to Nvidia chips to train powerful A.I. models. Ms. Huang’s network has been linked to efforts to supply the powerful chips to Chinese-state owned military contractors doing work for the People’s Liberation Army.
 
Little of the intelligence about Ms. Huang and her network has been provided to Capitol Hill, but lawmakers from both parties are demanding briefings.
 
A briefing this month for top lawmakers by John Ratcliffe, the C.I.A. director, and Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, was originally scheduled to discuss Iran, but The Times’s reporting on Nvidia led the lawmakers to ask questions about Mr. Huang and Alice Huang. Their answers raised more questions and left some lawmakers puzzled.
 
Trump administration officials postponed a follow-up briefing for top national security staffers scheduled for last Wednesday, in which senior officials were set to share details of the intelligence collected on Ms. Huang.
 
The intelligence about Ms. Huang was closely held inside the government until The Times reported the existence of the information in late October. Behind the scenes, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also the national security adviser, had written a confidential memo, dated March 30 this year, laying out Ms. Huang’s ties to Chinese intelligence.

data.title: Stocks to watch: Tata Steel, Waaree, Adani Energy, Maruti, IndusInd Bank
data.description:
Stocks to watch today: GIFT Nifty indicated a positive start for domestic indices on Monday as it traded 167.5 points, or 0.65 per cent, lower at 25,913 as of 07:42 AM.
 
Earlier on Friday, the Nifty 50 index closed 26.30 points, or 1.12 per cent, higher at 25,800.60. The 30-share BSE Sensex rallied 897.96 points, or 1.08 per cent, to settle at 83,919.71.
 
Meanwhile, Asian stocks were trading mixed, defying Friday’s moves on Wall Street. At the last check, South Korea's Kospi index was down 4.25 per cent, while Japan's Nikkei 225 was up 4.59 per cent. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 traded 0.08 per cent higher.
 
 
Overnight in the US, all three key Wall Street indices closed sharply lower. The Dow Jones Industrial Average tanked 1.93 per cent, the S&P 500 lost 3.7 per cent, and the Nasdaq Composite plummeted 5.28 per cent.
 
Oil prices stayed below $95 per barrel. Brent crude’s December futures were quoting at $92.29, down 0.30 per cent. WTI crude fell 0.22 per cent to $83.23 per barrel.
 
Stocks to watch
 
Tata Steel: The company has approved the sale of its tubes business and entire stake in Tata Steel Colours to APL Apollo Tubes in transactions valued at up to ₹28,000 crore, subject to regulatory clearances, with completion expected by March 2028. Waaree Energies: Its wholly owned subsidiary, Waaree Forever Energies, has signed a power purchase agreement (PPA) with SECI for a 700 MW solar project in Solapur, Maharashtra. The project also includes a 700 MW/2,800 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS).
 
Adani Energy Solutions: Subsidiary Powerpulse Trading Solutions has received a Letter of Award from WBSEDCL to supply 1,750 MW of round-the-clock renewable energy, along with an additional 750 MW under a greenshoe option.
 
Maruti Suzuki: The company has announced price hikes across select models with immediate effect. The weighted average increase is around 0.31 per cent to partially offset sustained input cost pressures.
 
IndusInd Bank: The bank’s board has decided to terminate former MD and CEO Sumant Kathpalia’s employment with immediate effect following an enquiry. It has also invoked applicable malus and clawback provisions retrospectively from March 24, 2020.
 
Premier Explosives: The company has secured an international export order worth $33.60 million (around ₹311 crore) for the manufacturing and supply of defence explosives.
 
RVNL: The company has emerged as the lowest bidder (L1) for a ₹348.49 crore East Coast Railway order to augment the Vadlapudi Wagon Workshop in Visakhapatnam.
 
Ratnaveer Precision Engineering: The company has secured long-term orders covering nearly 50 per cent of its upcoming copper clad laminate (CCL) manufacturing capacity. Its ₹338 crore capex project targets ₹750 crore in annual revenue and ₹150 crore in EBITDA at full capacity, with commercial production expected from February 2027.
 
Texmaco Rail & Engineering: The company has received two domestic letters of intent worth a combined ₹230.58 crore from JSW Group entities for manufacturing and supplying 553 wagons.
 
Aurobindo Pharma: The USFDA has issued an Establishment Inspection Report (EIR) with a Voluntary Action Indicated (VAI) classification for subsidiary Apitoria Pharma’s API facility, formally closing the August 2026 inspection that had resulted in three observations.
 
Cohance Lifesciences: The USFDA has issued an EIR with a VAI classification for its formulation manufacturing facility in Shamshabad, Telangana, formally concluding the earlier inspection.
 
Welspun Living: The company’s board has approved capital expenditure of up to ₹3,200 crore through its subsidiary, Welspun Home Solutions.
 
Arvind: The company has partnered with unspun to become the first manufacturer to deploy its OneWeave 3D weaving technology.
 
NATCO Pharma: The USFDA inspection at its Kothur facility in Hyderabad has concluded with seven Form 483 observations.
